knowledge.statement: End-to-end observation in a real three-node network: with the joint configuration active and the application caught up so that pendingConfIndex equals applied (2 and 2, already_pending false), an empty ConfChangeV2 whose transition is explicit was proposed and took the configuration-change path rather than being rewritten - the entry at index 3 read back as EntryConfChangeV2 and the commit index reached it (committed 3). Applying that committed entry the way an application must panicked with the error string config is already joint, and the configuration was still joint afterwards. The earlier variant of the same test, which proposed the same change without acknowledging applied entries, left the entry at index 3 as EntryNormal and therefore never reached the apply path, which is consistent with the pending-conf guard being the deciding factor in that run.

interpretations.rationale: Revision moving the end-to-end question from open to observed, with an explicit caveat about how the evidence was produced. Receipt 58945529ae764a599616bc1cf8629dd4 (experiment afeecd9696b540cc9850784dce4b18b4-experiment) ran in the isolated workspace; status completed, outcome tests_passed, exit 0, no changed target files, no parsing errors. Decisive parsed indices: 11 is the setup of the new test (StateLeader, joint true with voters [1 2 3] against outgoing [1 2 3], committed 2, applied 2, pending_conf_idx 2, already_pending false); 12 is the probe (entry_index 3, entry_type EntryConfChangeV2, committed 3, committed_reached true); 13 is the apply (panicked true, panic config is already joint, still_joint true). I read those raw events myself rather than relying on the comparison outcomes, which the controller recorded as unknown for all three: the diagnostics attribute that to my harness containing two network tests that emit identically named events, so the prerequisite association was ambiguous and the older test's setup event (indices 8-10) lacked the applicability field the prerequisite declared. That older test is the one whose malformed change was dropped as EntryNormal, and it remains in the receipt as an instructive contrast rather than as evidence. What is now established: in a real three-node cluster, once the application has acknowledged applied entries so no conf change is pending unapplied, an empty ConfChangeV2 with an explicit transition survives propose-time validation as an EntryConfChangeV2, commits, and panics the process when applied the way the API requires - so the defect is reachable through a genuine commit and not only by direct invocation. The asserted claim and its conditions stand: a joint configuration, no conf change pending unapplied, a caller-supplied non-Auto transition with zero changes, validation enabled, and an application that applies the committed entry rather than rejecting it; the Auto form remains the working control. Limits kept explicit: the comparisons in this receipt are unknown because of my event-name collision, so this is observed output plus source reasoning rather than a satisfied comparison; application progress was simulated with appliedTo rather than the full Ready and Advance loop; the consequence is a process panic in ApplyConfChange with no state corruption, data loss or safety violation claimed; and only the library's three transition values were covered, in one joint-configuration shape.
